The footnote on p. 1 calls it the author's version of the IUI '25 paper (30th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces, March 24-27, 2025, Cagliari, Italy), with the Version of Record at DOI 10.1145/3708359.3712094. Received 10 October 2024, accepted 12 December 2024 (p. 11). The retrieval record has no version_saved note.
source.title_on_document: One Does Not Simply Meme Alone: Evaluating Co-Creativity Between LLMs and Humans in the Generation of Humor

supplement.where: Called 'the supplementary material' (p. 5 and p. 6, Section 3.3). The document gives no URL.
supplement.holds: The full LLM prompts, including the system prompt of the chat assistant, and the full list of AI-generated captions. The document does not say it holds statistics. All printed statistics are in the main text, Figures 6-8, and Table 1. No arm means, SDs, or arm sizes are printed anywhere.

paper_design_summary: Prolific workers (124 recruited, 26 excluded for not completing, 98 analyzed) wrote captions for three meme template-topic combinations in one online session, either alone (human-only baseline) or with a GPT-4o chat panel during idea generation (human-AI collaboration), and a third condition had GPT-4o write captions with no person involved. The paper compares the number of ideas between the two human conditions, and a second Prolific sample (98 of 100 completed) rated 150 sampled memes per condition on how funny, creative, and shareable they were. The paper does not say how participants were allocated to the two human conditions.

studies.label: Meme creation: human only vs human-AI collaboration (GPT-4o chat during ideation), with crowd ratings of the memes

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: human only (baseline, no AI) or human-AI collaboration (GPT-4o chat panel during ideation). The paper calls it a between-subject study but does not say how participants were allocated to conditions. Randomization is named only for the image-topic permutation each participant received (p. 4, Section 3.2) and for 'randomization of tasks, etc.' on the server (p. 6, Section 3.4).
assignment.quote: we conducted a between-subject user study with three experimental groups.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3 (Methodology); random image-topic permutation: p. 4, Section 3.2; 'randomization of tasks, etc.': p. 6, Section 3.4

arms.name: Human only (baseline)
arms.description: Generated caption ideas, picked three favorites, and placed them on the meme template, with no AI tool or other help (p. 4, Section 3.1).

arms.name: Human-AI collaboration
arms.description: Same task, with a GPT-4o chat panel during the ideation step. Ideas in the model's responses were extracted automatically into the participant's idea list. Favorite selection and image creation had no AI (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 8, Section 5.1).

participants.exclusions: 124 recruited on Prolific, and 26 were excluded for not completing the task, which leaves 98 analyzed. The paper does not print 98: it is 124 minus 26, and it matches the 63 male + 35 female in Section 3.6 and the 882 favorites = 98 x 3 images x 3 favorites (p. 4). Arm sizes are not stated. The favorite counts imply 49 per arm (all 441 human-AI favorites = 49 x 9), but the paper does not give the split. The abstract's 'three groups of 50 participants each' (p. 1) conflicts with Section 3.6. The paper gives no n for any test, and the printed per-participant Mann-Whitney-U tests do not fit 49 per arm. As a consistency check (not recorded as data), the normal approximation at 49 vs 49 gives p of about 0.02 for the average number of ideas (W = 1519.5, printed p < 0.001), about 0.002 for the Effort item (W = 755, printed 0.027), and about 0.44 for the perceived number of ideas (W = 1308.5, printed 0.043), and a tie correction does not close these gaps. So the tests may not include all 98 people, or the arms may not hold 49 each. The printed statistics still need at least 78 people in the per-participant idea test (W = 1519.5 cannot exceed n1 x n2) and at least 91 in the Raw TLX test (the Welch df of 88.811 cannot exceed n1 + n2 - 2). For the ratings, technical problems left 415 of the baseline favorites usable and all 441 human-AI favorites. After dropping off-task captions, captions that hid most of the image, and one of six templates, 335 baseline and 307 human-AI memes remained, and 150 per arm were sampled (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2).
participants.who: Prolific workers with good English skills who had used an LLM interface at least once. 63 male and 35 female, mean age 28.8 (sd 8.7), from 30 countries. Paid the equivalent of 15 USD.
participants.quote: For this first part of the study, we recruited 124 participants using the online platform Prolific. 26 participants were excluded due to not completing the task.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 3.6; abstract, p. 1 ('three groups of 50'); favorites and curation, pp. 4-5, Section 3.2 and Figure 5; tests: p. 6, Section 4.1.1 and p. 7, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3

ai_tool.how_used: During the 4-5 minute ideation step for each image, participants could enter any prompt in a chat panel. A system prompt framed the model as a helper for meme ideas and capped each response at three ideas, and the current image was sent to the model before any user prompt. Ideas in the model's responses were extracted automatically into the participant's idea list. Favorite selection and image creation had no AI. Less than half of the participants interacted with the LLM more than once, and six had more than eight interactions (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Section 3.3; p. 6, Section 3.4; p. 8, Section 5.1; p. 9, Section 6.2).

task.description: Write captions for popular meme templates (baby, boromir, doge, futurama, toy-story; a sixth, 'choice', was excluded) on one of three topics (work, food, sports). For each of three image-topic combinations: generate as many captions as possible, pick three favorites, and place them on the template.
task.duration: At least four and at most five minutes of ideation per image. The whole session, survey included, was scheduled to take no more than 40 minutes (p. 4, Section 3.2).

outcomes.name: Crowd rating of meme creativity ('creative')
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: A second Prolific sample (100 recruited, 98 completed, each rating at least 50 images; mean age 32.6, sd 11.1; 29 countries; paid the equivalent of 10 USD) each saw a random 50 of the 450 memes and rated each on humor, creativity, and shareability. Rated memes: 10 per image-topic combination (5 templates x 3 topics), so 150 per condition. Rating scale not stated: Figure 8 axis ticks run 0 to 60, and the funny violins reach about 70. Three-condition ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise t-tests. The paper does not say whether the tests use single ratings or one score per meme. The printed Shapiro-Wilk results fit one score per meme (see reconciliation). Variants: per-topic reanalysis (Table 1) and the top four memes per dimension (Figure 1, p. 1; Section 5.3, p. 9), which is descriptive only.

contrasts.reported: Pairwise Bonferroni-adjusted t-test not significant, no statistic printed: 'Memes created by humans with the help of the LLM were not rated significantly different than those from the baseline'. Figure 8 has no bracket for this pair. Three-condition omnibus including AI only: ANOVA df = 2, F = 5.793, p = 0.003. By topic (Table 1): work KW chi2 = 11.22, p = 0.004; sports F = 2.095, p = 0.127; food F = 0.608, p = 0.546. No arm means, SDs, or ns printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 8; p. 8, Table 1

outcomes.name: Crowd rating of meme funniness ('funny')
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same raters, memes, and procedure as S1-O1. Raters judged how funny they found each meme (humor quality). Three-condition ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise t-tests. Scale and analysis unit not stated. Variants: per-topic reanalysis (Table 1) and the top four memes (Figure 1).

contrasts.reported: Pairwise Bonferroni-adjusted t-test not significant, no statistic printed (Section 4.2). Figure 8 has no bracket for this pair. Three-condition omnibus including AI only: ANOVA df = 2, F = 6.971, p = 0.001. By topic (Table 1): work F = 7.1, p = 0.001; sports F = 2.036, p = 0.134; food KW chi2 = 3.455, p = 0.177. No arm means, SDs, or ns printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 8; p. 8, Table 1

outcomes.name: Crowd rating of meme shareability ('shareable')
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same raters, memes, and procedure as S1-O1. Raters judged how likely they would be to share each meme. Not normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.988, p < 0.001 in the text; Table 1 prints p = 0.001), so Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise Mann-Whitney-U tests. Scale and analysis unit not stated. Variants: per-topic reanalysis (Table 1) and the top four memes (Figure 1).

contrasts.reported: Pairwise Bonferroni-adjusted Mann-Whitney-U test not significant, no statistic printed (Section 4.2). Figure 8 has no bracket for this pair. Three-condition omnibus including AI only: Kruskal-Wallis df = 2, chi2 = 11.761, p = 0.003. By topic (Table 1): work KW chi2 = 8.470, p = 0.014; sports F = 1.712, p = 0.184; food KW chi2 = 4.701, p = 0.095. No arm means, SDs, or ns printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 8; p. 8, Table 1

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated during ideation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of caption ideas in the participant's idea list during ideation. In the human-AI arm, ideas in the LLM's responses were extracted automatically into the list, so the count includes AI-supplied ideas (p. 4, Section 3.1). Two variants, each tested with a Mann-Whitney-U test after Shapiro-Wilk tests showed non-normality: the absolute number of ideas and the average number of ideas per participant. The unit 'participant' fits only the per-participant average (W = 1519.5). The paper gives no number of observations for either test. The absolute-count statistic (W = 12652) exceeds the largest value possible with 98 people in two arms (49 x 49 = 2401), so that test appears to use one row per participant and image. Figure 6 also appears to plot one count per participant and image: in the PDF's vector data every quartile, whisker end, and outlier falls on a whole number (human only: median 5, quartiles 4 and 6; human-AI: median 6, quartiles 4 and 9, outliers 18, 19, 19, 20, 21), and the text gives 21 as one participant's count for one image. As a consistency check (not recorded as data), neither printed p < 0.001 reproduces at the 49 per arm that the favorite counts imply: the normal approximation gives p of about 0.02 for W = 1519.5 at 49 vs 49 and about 0.01 for W = 12652 at 147 vs 147 rows. Pooled mean 6.1 ideas (sd 3.2), not split by arm. The text cites 'Figure 7' for the idea counts, but the idea-count plot is Figure 6.

contrasts.reported: Shapiro-Wilk: absolute number W = 0.811, p < 0.001; average per participant W = 0.820, p < 0.001. Mann-Whitney-U: absolute count W = 12652, p < 0.001; average number of ideas (1519.5, p < 0.001). Figure 6 box plots marked *** (p < 0.001). Pooled across arms: 6.1 ideas (sd: 3.2). No arm means, SDs, or ns printed.

company_involvement.description: Authors at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, LMU Munich, and TU Darmstadt. Funded by HumanE-AI-Net (Grant Agreement ID 952026). GPT-4o was used through the OpenAI API. The paper states no company role.

eligibility.reason: S1 compares people who worked alone with people who could prompt GPT-4o, in a 'between-subject user study with three experimental groups' (p. 4, Section 3), but the paper never says how participants were allocated to the two human conditions. Randomization is named only for image-topic permutations (p. 4, Section 3.2) and for 'randomization of tasks, etc.' (p. 6, Section 3.4). If allocation was random, S1 is an online_rct with ai_vs_bau contrasts and enters the core. If it was not, S1 is observational context (quasi_people). Criterion 2: 98 people analyzed across the two human arms (124 recruited minus 26 non-completers, p. 6, Section 3.6), well above 50. The split by arm is not stated, the favorite counts imply 49 per arm, and the abstract's 'groups of 50' (p. 1) conflicts with Section 3.6. The printed per-participant Mann-Whitney-U tests do not fit 49 per arm, so they may not include all 98 people, but the printed statistics still need at least 78 people in the per-participant idea test and at least 91 in the Raw TLX test (pp. 6-7, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2), so criterion 2 is met under any reading. Criterion 3: crowd ratings of the memes and idea counts are scored on the output. S2 (AI-only memes vs human memes) is ai_vs_human context.

one_line_finding: People who could prompt GPT-4o while generating captions listed more ideas than people working alone (Mann-Whitney-U W = 12652 for the absolute count and 1519.5 for the per-participant average, both p < 0.001, p. 6, Section 4.1.1 and Figure 6), but their memes were not rated significantly different on funniness, creativity, or shareability (no pairwise statistics printed, p. 7, Section 4.2 and Figure 8), while AI-only memes were rated higher than human-only memes on all three and higher than human-AI memes on funniness and creativity (Figure 8 stars, p. 7; three-condition creativity ANOVA F = 5.793, p = 0.003, p. 8, Table 1).
open_questions: How were participants allocated to the human-only and human-AI conditions? The paper names randomization only for image-topic permutations and for 'randomization of tasks, etc.' The ACM Version of Record (DOI 10.1145/3708359.3712094) was not compared with this file.

How many of the 98 analyzed participants were in each arm, and how many entered each test? The abstract says 'three groups of 50 participants each'. The favorite counts (all 441 human-AI favorites usable, nine favorites per person) imply 49 per arm, but the paper does not state the split, and the printed per-participant Mann-Whitney-U results (W = 1519.5, 755, and 1308.5) do not give the printed p-values at 49 vs 49.

Were the rating tests run on single ratings or on one score per meme, how were the ratings of a meme combined, and on what scale? The printed Shapiro-Wilk results fit tests on 450 memes (150 per topic). Error degrees of freedom are not printed.

What are the rows and n of the Mann-Whitney test on the absolute idea count (W = 12652)? The value exceeds what 98 people in two arms could produce, so the test likely uses one row per participant and image, as Figure 6 appears to. Even at 147 rows per arm, W = 12652 gives p of about 0.01, not the printed p < 0.001.
No pairwise rating statistics, arm means, or SDs are printed for any contrast. Effect sizes would need the authors' data.
How many distinct S1 participants contributed the 150 sampled memes per arm? Some baseline favorites were lost to technical problems (415 of 441 usable).
notes: Self-reported outcomes are not listed because they are not scored on the output: raw NASA-TLX, no significant difference (t = -0.955, df = 88.811, p = 0.342); the 'Effort' item, lower with the LLM (Mann-Whitney-U W = 755, p = 0.027); perceived number of ideas, higher with the LLM (W = 1308.5, p = 0.043); perceived ownership, lower with the LLM (W = 562, p < 0.001) (pp. 6-7, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3, Figure 7). No diversity or similarity outcome is reported. Figure 8 marks were read from the PDF's vector data, with each bracket's end points matched to the violin centers and each star centered on its bracket. Funny: human-only vs AI-only ** and human-AI vs AI-only *. Creative: human-only vs AI-only * and human-AI vs AI-only **. Shareable: human-only vs AI-only * only. No bracket joins the two human arms. The Figure 8 caption lists '**: p < 0.001' after '**: p < 0.01', apparently a typo for ***. Table 1 underlines, which mark Kruskal-Wallis tests, sit under 11.761 (all topics, shareable), 11.22 and 8.470 (work, creative and shareable), and 3.455 and 4.701 (food, funny and shareable), located in the PDF's vector data. Table 1 prints the shareability Shapiro-Wilk p as 0.001, and the text prints p < 0.001. The paper mentions a power analysis but gives no details (p. 6, Section 3.6). The markdown conversion scrambles Section 4.2 and Table 1, so all numbers were checked against PDF pp. 6-8. This file replaces an earlier reconciliation of c168 built from a different pair of screener forms.

differences.field: studies[S1].outcomes[S1-O1 creative, S1-O2 funny, S1-O3 shareable].unit and studies[S2].outcomes[S2-O1, S2-O2, S2-O3].unit

differences.b: output (n_units 300 for the S1 outcomes, 450 for the S2 outcomes)
differences.resolved: Provisional 'output' (B), with n_units unchanged at 300 for S1 (150 baseline + 150 human-AI memes) and 450 for S2 (150 per condition). The paper never states whether its tests use single ratings or one score per meme. A's 'rating' cannot carry n_units 300, because 98 raters gave at least 50 ratings each. Check: under the Royston normalization that R and SciPy use, all 12 printed Shapiro-Wilk results reproduce at one score per meme (n = 450 overall and 150 per topic; W = 0.995 gives p = 0.155, as printed) and would fall below 1e-7 at single ratings (about 4,900 overall). Missing: a statement of the analysis unit, how the ratings of each meme were combined, the rating scale, and the error degrees of freedom.
differences.quote: the data from the “funny” and “creative” scale were likely normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk test: W = 0.994, p = 0.062 and W = 0.995, p = 0.155 respectively)
differences.locator: p. 7, Section 4.2; p. 8, Table 1 (Shapiro-Wilk columns); p. 5, Section 3.2 (150 memes per condition); p. 6, Section 3.6 (98 raters, at least 50 images each)

differences.resolved: yes (B). The rated captions were written during ideation, when the human-AI arm had the GPT-4o chat panel and the model's ideas went straight into the idea list. Only the choice of three favorites and their placement on the template, in the same session, ran without AI, and measure_detail and ai_tool record this. Both forms code these outcomes with_ai, which the codebook ties to output produced with AI available. In this screening 'mixed' marks AI output compared with human output (c003, c007, c014, c017), and an AI arm against a no-AI arm is coded 'yes' (c013, c082).
differences.quote: AI assistance mainly contributed during the idea generation stage, whereas in the stages of idea screening and creating the meme image, no AI assistance or suggestions were provided.
differences.locator: p. 8, Section 5.1; p. 4, Section 3.1 (chat panel in the ideation step)

differences.resolved: mixed (A). The S2 contrasts compare memes written by GPT-4o with no person involved against memes made without AI (baseline) and memes made with the chat panel (human-AI). No person in the AI-only condition worked with AI. This matches the other reconciled AI-versus-human outcomes (c003, c007, c014, c017).

Figure 8 gives only a Bonferroni-adjusted significance level (* or **) and each arm's distribution. differences.a: Participants with a GPT-4o chat assistant produced more caption ideas (Mann-Whitney W = 12652, p < 0.001; p. 6, Figure 6), but crowd ratings of their memes on funny, creative, and shareable did not differ from human-only memes, while AI-only memes were rated higher than both (Figure 8, p. 7; Table 1, p. 8).
differences.b: Participants with a GPT-4o chat generated more caption ideas than unassisted participants (Mann-Whitney W = 12652, p < 0.001; p. 6, Fig. 6), but their memes were not rated differently on funny, creative, or shareable, while AI-only memes were rated higher than both human conditions (omnibus F = 6.971, 5.793, chi2 = 11.761; p. 7 Fig. 8, p. 8 Table 1).
differences.resolved: Neither form exactly. Both say AI-only memes were rated higher than both human conditions, but the AI-only vs human-AI comparison was not significant for shareability. The final sentence also adds the per-participant idea statistic (1519.5), says 'not significantly different' as the paper does, and keeps one omnibus number.
differences.quote: The only exception to this was “shareability” where the comparison between the cooperative and pure AI creation was not significant.

challenge_resolution.problem: The conclusion under test reads S1 as a randomized experiment, but no sentence in the PDF says how the creators were allocated to the human-only and human-AI conditions. Randomization of creators is named only for the image-topic permutation inside a condition and for 'randomization of tasks, etc.' on the server.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: No change. The form already codes S1 randomized 'not_stated', design_class 'other', criterion 1 'unclear', and core 'unclear', which is the checker's own conclusion. A search of the PDF text layer (pp. 1-11) for random*, assign*, allocat*, and counterbalanc* finds randomization only for the image-topic permutation (p. 4), the sampling of memes and of the images shown to raters (p. 5), 'randomization of tasks, etc.' (p. 6), and 'random users from a crowdsourcing platform' (p. 9). The allocation question stays open and is the one open item that affects eligibility.
challenge_resolution.quote: The permutation of image and topic was selected randomly but in a way that each participant used each image and each topic at most once.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 4, Section 3 and Section 3.2; p. 5, Figure 4; p. 6, Section 3.4; text layer of PDF pp. 1-11

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O4 (number of ideas) is coded unit 'participant', but only the per-participant average test (W = 1519.5) uses one row per participant. The absolute-count test (W = 12652) and Figure 6 use one value per participant and image, and neither printed p < 0.001 reproduces at 49 per arm.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: studies[S1].outcomes[S1-O4].measure_detail now says that 'participant' fits only the per-participant average, that Figure 6 appears to plot one count per participant and image (every quartile, whisker end, and outlier falls on a whole number in the PDF's vector data, and the highest point, 21, equals the text's maximum for one participant on one image), and that, as a consistency check, the normal approximation gives p of about 0.02 for W = 1519.5 at 49 vs 49 and about 0.01 for W = 12652 at 147 vs 147 rows. Open question 4 says the same. unit stays 'participant', n_units stays null, and the reported string is unchanged because it records the printed labels.

challenge_resolution.problem: The rating outcomes (S1-O1 to S1-O3 and S2-O1 to S2-O3) are coded unit 'output', but no sentence says whether the ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, and pairwise tests use single ratings or one score per meme, how a meme's ratings were combined, or what the rating scale was. The code rests on the printed Shapiro-Wilk results.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: No coded value changed. unit stays 'output' (n_units 300 for S1 and 450 for S2) as a provisional code, because the unit field has no not_stated option and the inference is strong: recomputed with the Royston approximation, all 12 Shapiro-Wilk p-values in Table 1 fall inside the range their rounded W implies at n = 450 overall and 150 per topic, and each would be below 1e-11 at single ratings (about 4,900). The S1 rating outcomes already say the unit is not stated. The S2 rating outcomes' measure_detail now says so too. The reconciliation difference on this unit stays unresolved and is an open item.

challenge_resolution.problem: The form treats 98 analyzed and an implied 49 per arm as consistent, but the printed per-participant Mann-Whitney-U statistics cannot come from 49 + 49 people, so fewer than 98 people entered the tests or the arms were unequal. The form did not flag this.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: participants.exclusions, eligibility.reason, and open question 2 now flag the conflict. As a consistency check (not recorded as data), the normal approximation at 49 vs 49 gives p of about 0.02 for W = 1519.5 (printed p < 0.001), about 0.002 for W = 755 (printed 0.027), and about 0.44 for W = 1308.5 (printed 0.043). The same fields record the lower bounds that keep criterion 2 met under any reading: at least 78 people in the per-participant idea test (W cannot exceed n1 x n2) and at least 91 in the Raw TLX test (Welch df 88.811 cannot exceed n1 + n2 - 2). n_analyzed stays 98, the count after the 26 stated exclusions, and the participants locator now cites the test pages. Separately, to follow the spec's wording rule, paper_design_summary and participants.exclusions now say '98 analyzed'. The reconciliation object is unchanged, so its agreed_fields_checked entry that confirms 98 predates this flag.
challenge_resolution.quote: This test indicated significant differences for the absolute count (W = 12652, p < 0.001) and the average number of ideas (1519.5, p < 0.001).

open_items.item: Allocation to conditions (open question 1): the paper calls S1 a 'between-subject user study with three experimental groups' but never says how people were allocated to the human-only and human-AI conditions. If allocation was random, S1 is an online_rct and the paper enters the core. If it was not, S1 is observational context. arXiv v2 calls itself the author's version of the IUI '25 paper, and the ACM Version of Record (DOI 10.1145/3708359.3712094) was not compared. If the journal version does not say, the authors.

Arm sizes and the n in each test (open question 2): the favorite counts imply 49 per arm, the abstract says 'three groups of 50', and the printed per-participant Mann-Whitney-U statistics do not fit 49 vs 49. Criterion 2 is met under any reading: 98 analyzed after the stated exclusions, and the printed statistics need at least 78 people in the per-participant idea test. The arm sizes matter for n_treatment and n_control.

Unit of the rating analyses (open question 3 and the one unresolved reconciliation difference): single ratings or one score per meme, how each meme's ratings were combined, the rating scale, and the error degrees of freedom. 'output' is provisional, and all 12 Shapiro-Wilk results fit one score per meme. Criterion 3 holds either way, because the ratings score the memes.

Rows and n of the idea-count tests (open question 4): W = 12652 exceeds 49 x 49, Figure 6 appears to plot one count per participant and image, and neither printed p < 0.001 reproduces at 49 per arm. This decides which statistic extraction can use, not eligibility.
No pairwise rating statistics, arm means, or SDs are printed for any contrast, and the document names no posted data or code (open question 5). Effect sizes need the authors' data.

How many distinct S1 participants made the 150 sampled memes per arm (open question 6). Criterion 2 counts the 98 people analyzed in S1 and does not depend on it. The count matters for the people-level n of the rating contrasts.
